posts.title: EEG Preprocessing: A Simple Step-by-Step Guide
content: By Md Shaheen Perwez.

Electroencephalography (EEG) is a powerful and safe way to record the brain's electrical activity, but it can easily pick up unwanted noise (Delorme, 2023). Because the recording sensors are placed on the scalp's surface, the weak brain signals must travel through the brain's protective layers and the skull, making the data highly vulnerable to interference from the room's environment and the person's own body movements (Liu et al., 2005). To get clear, useful information from raw EEG recordings - whether you are building a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) or studying how people imagine movements - researchers use a strict cleaning process called "preprocessing" (Bigdely-Shamlo et al., 2015). Here is a simple breakdown of the standard EEG cleaning pipeline.
Frequency Filtering: Removing Drifts and Interference
The very first step to clean the data is to apply frequency filters, which block out signal changes that have absolutely nothing to do with brain activity (Delorme, 2023).
High-Pass Filtering

This removes slow, rolling noises, such as those caused by sweating or changes in the way the sensors contact the skin. Applying a 0.5 Hz high-pass filter is generally considered the best way to remove these slow drifts without warping the important brain event data you want to study (Tanner et al., 2016).
Notch Filtering and Spatial-Spectral Algorithms

Normal electrical devices in the room produce a specific hum at 50 Hz or 60 Hz. In the past, researchers removed this by using a "notch filter," which simply cuts a hole in the data at that exact frequency. Today, modern cleaning pipelines use smarter algorithms like ZapLine, which carefully estimate and remove only the electrical hum without losing real brain data or smearing the signal (de Cheveigne, 2020; Klug & Kloosterman, 2022).
Re-Referencing

EEG sensors measure the electrical difference between two points, meaning the reference point you choose completely changes how the brain signals look across the head (Lei & Liao, 2017). A widely accepted method is the Common Average Reference (CAR). This method calculates the average signal across all sensors and subtracts it from each individual sensor, which effectively suppresses noise shared across the scalp (Zheng et al., 2018). Alternatively, a surface Laplacian spatial filter can be used. This filter zooms in on very specific, local brain activity by calculating the difference between one specific channel and its closest physical neighbours (Kayser & Tenke, 2015).
Rejecting Biological Artefacts

Things the body does naturally, like blinking, heartbeats, and clenching the jaw or neck muscles, create massive electrical spikes that are up to ten times larger than true brain signals (Delorme, 2023).
Independent Component Analysis (ICA)

ICA is the gold standard for removing these body noises. It uses advanced math to untangle the jumbled, multichannel EEG data into separate, independent signal components (Delorme & Makeig, 2004). Once the data is untangled, the specific components that look and act like blinks or heartbeats can be deleted, and the remaining clean brain components are put back together.
Automated Classification

To avoid human error and bias when manually guessing which components are noise, modern pipelines use machine-learning plugins such as ADJUST and ICLabel. These computer programs automatically identify and discard noisy components based on their appearance and timing (Mognon et al., 2011; Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019).
Epoching and Baseline Correction

Once the long, continuous EEG stream is cleaned, it is chopped up into smaller, bite-sized time windows known as "epochs" or "trials." These small windows are time-locked to a specific event, like when a picture flashes on a screen or a person begins to move (Delorme, 2023). Historically, the final step of this process was "baseline correction," which meant finding a quiet resting period right before the event, calculating its average voltage, and subtracting that average from the entire trial to level it out (Delorme, 2023). However, recent studies have discovered a major catch: if the raw data has already been high-pass filtered at 0.5 Hz to correct for slow drifts, applying a traditional baseline correction on top can actually warp the data and significantly reduce the accuracy of your results (Tanner et al., 2016). Because of this, many modern pipelines now skip baseline removal entirely to preserve the brain's true electrical dynamics (Delorme, 2023).
